item.title: Simply-Typed λ-Calculus
item.description:
In our Church encoding lecture, we saw that the λ-calculus can encode numbers, booleans, lists, and recursion. But we also saw a problem: there’s nothing stopping you from writing nonsense like (+ 1 #f). It encodes just fine, but reduces to garbage. In this lecture, we introduce type systems: a formal mechanism for ruling out programs that would exhibit runtime type errors.

Why Type Systems?

Consider the following expressions. Which ones should be allowed to run?

(λ (g) (g 5))
((λ (f x) (f x)) g)
(λ (f) (+ (f 1) (if (= 0 (string-length (f 1))) 1 0)))

The first looks fine: nothing obviously wrong, as long as g is a function that can accept 5. The second is problematic: it takes two arguments, so ((λ (f x) (f x)) g) only passes one, and (f x) tries to call g as a function with whatever x is. The third is deeply broken: (f 1) would need to return both a number (for +) and a string (for string-length).

A type system assigns each subexpression a type, a rough approximation of how it will behave at runtime. For example, int represents integers, and int → int represents functions from integers to integers. The goal: rule out programs that would crash with a type error, before we even run them.

QuickAnswer

In Racket, what happens if you evaluate (+ 1 #t)? At what point does the error occur: compile time or runtime?

The Simply-Typed λ-Calculus

The Simply-Typed Lambda Calculus (STLC) is a restriction of the untyped λ-calculus. Not all untyped terms are well-typed: STLC rejects programs that could go wrong. This is deliberate. By restricting which programs can be written, we gain a guarantee: every well-typed program is safe.

Term syntax

STLC extends the λ-calculus with type annotations on lambda parameters:

e ::= (λ (x : τ) e)    – annotated lambda
    | (e e)             – application
    | x                 – variable
    | n                 – integer literal
    | b                 – boolean literal (#t, #f)
    | (+ e e)           – addition
    | (- e)             – negation
    | (if0 e e e)       – conditional (if first arg is 0)
    | (let ([x e]) e)   – let binding

The key difference from the untyped λ-calculus: every lambda must annotate its parameter with a type. This is what makes type checking straightforward.

Type syntax

Types in STLC are simple:

τ ::= int              – integers
    | bool             – booleans
    | τ → τ            – function types

The arrow type τ₁ → τ₂ describes functions that accept an argument of type τ₁ and return a result of type τ₂. Arrow is right-associative: int → int → int means int → (int → int).

QuickAnswer

What is the type of a function that takes an integer and returns a function from integers to integers? Write it using the arrow notation.

QuickAnswer

What is the type of (λ (x : int) (λ (y : bool) y))? (Hint: the outer lambda takes an int, the inner returns a bool.)

The Typing Judgement

We express “expression e has type τ” using a typing judgement:

Γ ⊢ e : τ

This reads: “under the typing environment Γ, expression e has type τ.” The environment Γ maps variables to their types, just as our interpreter environments mapped variables to values. For a closed term (no free variables), Γ is empty.

For example:

  • ⊢ 42 : int says “42 has type int” (empty environment)
  • x : int ⊢ x : int says “assuming x is an int, x has type int”
  • ⊢ (λ (x : int) x) : int → int says “the identity function on ints has type int → int”

We prove these judgements using natural deduction rules, just as we did for evaluation in our closures lecture. Each rule tells us how to conclude that an expression has a certain type, based on the types of its subexpressions.

Typing Rules

Literals: T-Int and T-Bool

The simplest rules. A literal integer has type int, a literal boolean has type bool, regardless of the environment:

These rules have no premises (nothing above the line). They are axioms: you can always conclude that a number is an int.

QuickAnswer

Using the T-Int rule, what is the type of 42? What about -7? Does the environment matter?

Variables: T-Var

To type a variable, we look it up in the environment:

Side condition: (x : τ) ∈ Γ

This says: if the environment maps x to type τ, then x has type τ. The side condition is critical: if x is not in Γ, the variable is unbound and the term is ill-typed.

QuickAnswer

Using T-Var, complete this judgement:

{x : int, y : bool} ⊢ y : ???

QuickAnswer

Can we derive a type for x under the empty environment {}? Why or why not?

Functions: T-Lam

This is the central rule. It says: if, assuming x has type τ₁, you can show the body e has type τ₂, then the whole lambda has type τ₁ → τ₂:

The notation Γ, x:τ₁ means “extend Γ with the binding x : τ₁.” Because the lambda is annotated with τ₁, we don’t have to guess the type of x: it’s written right there in the syntax.

Let’s prove that (λ (x : int) x) has type int → int. Click to load this into the proof explorer and try building the derivation:

⊢ (λ (x : int) x) : int → int

The completed derivation looks like this:

Reading bottom-up: we want to show ⊢ (λ (x : int) x) : int → int. By T-Lam, we need to show x : int ⊢ x : int. By T-Var (since x : int is in the environment), this holds.

QuickAnswer

What is the type of (λ (x : int) 42)? Build the typing derivation.

Application: T-App

To type a function application, we need the function to have an arrow type, and the argument to match the input type:

This is where type checking catches errors. If e₁ has type int → bool but e₂ has type bool, the types don’t match (we need e₂ : int) and the application is ill-typed.

Let’s prove that ((λ (x : int) x) 5) has type int. Click to try:

⊢ ((λ (x : int) x) 5) : int

The completed derivation:

Notice how T-App requires two premises: one for the function, one for the argument. The key constraint is that the argument type τ₁ must match in both premises.

QuickAnswer

Try building the derivation for the following in the proof explorer:

⊢ ((λ (f : int → int) (f 1)) (λ (x : int) x)) : int

Arithmetic: T-Add and T-Neg

Addition requires both arguments to be integers:

Negation takes one integer argument:

QuickAnswer

Build the derivation for:

x : int ⊢ (+ x 1) : int

Conditionals: T-If

Our conditional is if0: it tests whether its first argument is zero. Both branches must have the same type:

The condition e₁ must be an integer (we test if it’s zero), and both branches e₂ and e₃ must have the same type τ. This prevents the problem from the motivation: we can’t have one branch return an int and the other return a bool.

QuickAnswer

Why does STLC require both branches of if0 to have the same type? What would go wrong if we allowed (if0 0 42 #t)?

Let bindings: T-Let

The T-Let rule binds a variable for use in the body:

First, type check e₁ to get its type τ₁. Then, type check the body e₂ with x : τ₁ added to the environment.

QuickAnswer

Build the derivation for:

⊢ (let ([x 5]) (+ x 1)) : int

Building Complete Derivations

Now that we have all the rules, let’s practice building complete derivations. The key skill is working bottom-up: start with the conclusion you want to prove, identify which rule applies (based on the outermost form of the expression), and generate the premises.

Example: a higher-order function

Let’s type (λ (f : int → int) (f 1)). This takes a function f and applies it to 1. Click to try:

⊢ (λ (f : int → int) (f 1)) : (int → int) → int

The derivation:

Notice the type of the whole expression: (int → int) → int. This is a function that takes a function as input, making it higher-order.

QuickAnswer

What is the type of (λ (f : int → int) (λ (x : int) (f (f x))))? This is a function that applies f twice. Build the derivation in the proof explorer.

⊢ (λ (f : int → int) (λ (x : int) (f (f x)))) : (int → int) → int → int

What STLC Can’t Type

STLC is deliberately less expressive than the untyped λ-calculus. Some important terms cannot be typed:

Self-application is untypable. Consider (λ (f) (f f)). For this to type check, f would need to have type τ → τ' (so we can apply it), but also type τ (since it’s the argument). So we’d need τ = τ → τ', which is an infinite type: no finite type works.

Ω is untypable. Since (λ (x) (x x)) can’t be typed, neither can ((λ (x) (x x)) (λ (x) (x x))). This means the term that loops forever is rejected by STLC.

The Y combinator is untypable. Since the Y combinator uses self-application internally, STLC rejects it. This means we cannot write general recursion in STLC.

This is a feature, not a bug. In fact, every well-typed STLC program is guaranteed to terminate. The price we pay for this safety is that we can’t express some useful programs (like recursive functions). More advanced type systems, such as System F and those in OCaml or Haskell, recover expressiveness while maintaining safety by adding controlled forms of polymorphism and recursion.

QuickAnswer

Why can’t (λ (f : ???) (f f)) be typed in STLC, no matter what type we write for ????

Type Soundness (Preview)

The payoff of type systems is a strong guarantee:

Theorem (Type Soundness): Well-typed programs don’t go wrong.

This is traditionally split into two properties:

  • Progress: If ⊢ e : τ (i.e., e is well-typed and closed), then either e is already a value, or e can take a step of evaluation.

  • Preservation: If ⊢ e : τ and e steps to e', then ⊢ e' : τ. Evaluation preserves the type.

Together, these say: a well-typed program never reaches a stuck state (like trying to add a boolean to a number). It either produces a value or keeps computing, and its type never changes along the way.

We will not prove type soundness in this class, but it is the foundational result that justifies type systems.

QuickAnswer

What does “progress” guarantee about the expression ((λ (x : int) (+ x 1)) 5) if it type checks?

From Rules to Code

A beautiful property of STLC: the typing rules are syntax-directed. Each rule applies to exactly one syntactic form (T-Int for integers, T-Lam for lambdas, T-App for applications, etc.). This means we can implement type checking as a simple recursive function over the expression. In this section we will build a nearly-complete type checker for STLC in Racket.

Representing types and expressions

First, we need predicates that recognize valid STLC types and expressions. Types are either base types (int, bool) or arrow types:

(define (type? t)
  (match t
    ['int #t]
    ['bool #t]
    [`(,(? type? t0) -> ,(? type? t1)) #t]
    [_ #f]))

So 'int is a type, '(int -> bool) is a type, and '((int -> int) -> (bool -> (int -> int))) is a type. Arrow is represented as a two-element list with -> in the middle.

Expressions include variables, literals, annotated lambdas, applications, and type annotations on arbitrary subexpressions:

(define (expr? e)
  (match e
    [(? symbol? x) #t]
    [(? boolean? b) #t]
    [(? integer? i) #t]
    [`(,(? expr? e0) ,(? expr? e1)) #t]
    [`(,(? expr? e) : ,(? type? t)) #t]
    [`(lambda (,(? symbol? x) : ,(? type? t)) ,(? expr? e)) #t]))

Notice two things. First, lambda parameters must carry type annotations: (lambda (x : int) x) rather than (lambda (x) x). This is what makes type checking (as opposed to type inference) straightforward. Second, any subexpression can be annotated with a type via (e : t), which serves as an explicit type ascription that the checker must verify.

Type synthesis

The core of our type checker is synthesize-type: given a typing environment env (a hash mapping variable names to types) and an expression e, it returns the type of e, or raises an error if the expression is ill-typed.

Because the rules are syntax-directed, each match case corresponds to exactly one typing rule:

(define (synthesize-type env e)
  (match e
    ;; T-Int: integer literals have type int
    [(? integer? i) 'int]
    ;; T-Bool: boolean literals have type bool
    [(? boolean? b) 'bool]
    ;; T-Var: look up the variable in the environment
    [(? symbol? x) (hash-ref env x)]
    ;; T-Lam: extend the environment and synthesize the body
    [`(lambda (,x : ,A) ,e-body)
     (define B (synthesize-type (hash-set env x A) e-body))
     `(,A -> ,B)]
    ;; Type ascription: synthesize, then check it matches
    [`(,e : ,t)
     (let ([e-t (synthesize-type env e)])
       (if (equal? e-t t)
           t
           (error (format "types ~a and ~a are different" e-t t))))]
    ;; T-App: application
    [`(,e1 ,e2)
     'todo]))

The literal cases are axioms: integers are int, booleans are bool. The variable case is T-Var: look up the variable in env. The lambda case is T-Lam: extend the environment with x : A and recursively synthesize the body’s type B, returning the arrow type (A -> B). The annotation case synthesizes a type for the inner expression and verifies it matches the annotation.

QuickAnswer

The application case is left as ???. Using the T-App rule as a guide, implement it. You need to: (1) synthesize the type of e1, (2) check that it is an arrow type, (3) synthesize the type of e2, (4) check that it matches the arrow’s input type, and (5) return the arrow’s output type. Raise an error on a mismatch.

Wiring up the initial environment

Our language includes two built-in operations: + (curried addition) and is-zero? (integer test). Rather than adding special typing rules for these, we simply put them in the initial environment with the right types:

(define (synthesize-stlc-type e)
  (synthesize-type (hash '+ '(int -> (int -> int))
                         'is-zero? '(int -> bool))
                   e))

Notice that + is curried: it takes an int, returns a function (int -> int). So (+ 3) has type (int -> int), and ((+ 3) 4) has type int. This means addition is written as ((+ e1) e2) in our syntax.

Let’s test it:

(synthesize-stlc-type '((lambda (x : int) x) 23))
;; => 'int

(synthesize-stlc-type '(lambda (x : int)
                         (lambda (y : bool)
                           (lambda (z : int) x))))
;; => '(int -> (bool -> (int -> int)))

Type checking as a wrapper

Once we can synthesize types, checking is trivial: synthesize and compare:

(define (check-stlc-type e t)
  'todo)

QuickAnswer

Implement check-stlc-type. It takes an expression e and a type t, and returns #t if e has type t, #f otherwise. (Hint: this is a one-liner using synthesize-stlc-type and equal?.)

Type erasure

Here is the key insight connecting our type checker to actual execution: STLC terms are just λ-calculus terms with extra annotations. Once we know a program is well-typed, we can erase all the type annotations and run the result as plain Racket:

(define (erase-types e)
  (match e
    ;; + is curried in STLC but not in Racket
    [`((+ ,e0) ,e1) `(+ ,(erase-types e0) ,(erase-types e1))]
    ;; Drop the type annotation from lambdas
    [`(lambda (,x : ,t) ,e-body) `(lambda (,x) ,(erase-types e-body))]
    ;; Variables and literals pass through unchanged
    [(? symbol? x) x]
    [(? boolean? b) b]
    [(? integer? i) i]
    ;; Drop type ascriptions
    [`(,e : ,t) (erase-types e)]
    ;; Recurse into applications
    [`(,e0 ,e1) `(,(erase-types e0) ,(erase-types e1))]))

The lambda case drops : t from the parameter. The ascription case (e : t) strips the annotation entirely. The + case uncurries ((+ e0) e1) back into Racket’s (+ e0 e1).

The full pipeline: STLC to Racket

Putting it all together, we can compile STLC to Racket by first type checking, then erasing types. If the type checker raises an error, we catch it and return 'type-error:

(define (stlc->racket e)
  (with-handlers ([exn:fail? (lambda (exn) 'type-error)])
    (synthesize-stlc-type e)
    (erase-types e)))

This gives us a complete pipeline. Well-typed programs get compiled to executable Racket, ill-typed programs are rejected:

(stlc->racket '((lambda (x : int) x) 23))
;; => '((lambda (x) x) 23)
;; evaluates to 23

(stlc->racket '(lambda (x : (int -> int))
                 (lambda (y : bool)
                   (lambda (z : int) (x y)))))
;; => 'type-error
;; because y : bool but x expects an int

The structure of the code mirrors the structure of the proof. This is a recurring theme in programming languages: proofs and programs are deeply connected.

QuickAnswer

Trace through what stlc->racket does on '(lambda (x : int) ((+ x) 1)). What does synthesize-stlc-type return? What does erase-types produce?

Summary

Concept Key idea
Types Rough approximation of runtime behavior
Typing judgement Γ ⊢ e : τ: “under Γ, e has type τ”
Environment Γ Maps variables to their types
Typing rules Natural deduction rules, one per syntactic form
Type soundness Well-typed programs don’t go wrong
STLC limitations Can’t type self-application, Ω, or Y
Syntax-directed One rule per form, so type checking is a recursive function
Type erasure Once checked, strip annotations and run as untyped code

The STLC is the foundation of type systems in modern functional languages. In our next lecture, we’ll study type inference: how to automatically deduce types without requiring annotations, using Hindley-Milner type inference as implemented in languages like OCaml, Haskell, and Rust.

item.title: Type Soundness for STLC
item.description:
Companion to the STLC lecture. Read that first.

In the STLC lecture, we claimed that well-typed programs don’t go wrong. In this lecture, we make that claim precise and prove it. The proof has two parts, progress and preservation, proved by induction over the typing derivation. We will also develop the proof in Lean4, a proof assistant where the computer checks every step of our reasoning.

The emphasis throughout is on why each step works, not just the formal mechanics. If you find yourself losing the forest for the trees, come back to this: type soundness says that evaluation never produces a nonsensical state. Progress says you’re never stuck. Preservation says you never drift off course.

What Does “Safe” Mean?

A term is stuck if it is not a value and cannot take a step. For example, (5 3) is stuck in the untyped λ-calculus: 5 is not a function, so we can’t β-reduce, and it’s not a value either. Stuck terms are the runtime type errors we want to prevent.

Type soundness says: if a term is well-typed, it never gets stuck. No matter how many steps of evaluation we take, we either reach a value or we can keep going.

This decomposes into two properties:

  • Progress: a well-typed closed term is either a value or can step. (“You can always make a move.”)

  • Preservation: if a well-typed term steps, the result is still well-typed at the same type. (“You stay on the right track.”)

Together: you can always make a move (progress), and each move keeps your type the same (preservation), so you never arrive at a stuck state with a bad type.

QuickAnswer

Give an example of a stuck term in the untyped λ-calculus. Why is it stuck? (Hint: try applying a non-function to something.)

Lean4 Definitions: Syntax, Typing, Semantics

Before the proofs, let’s see the full system in Lean4. Every definition here corresponds to something from the STLC lecture. Lean4 is a dependently-typed language: it can express propositions as types and proofs as programs. We define our STLC system as inductive data types, then prove properties about them using tactics.

Types

Types are int, bool, or function types τ₁ ⇒ τ₂:

inductive Ty : Type where
  | int  : Ty
  | bool : Ty
  | arrow : Ty → Ty → Ty
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

De Bruijn indices: how variables work

In the STLC lecture, we used named variables: (λ (x : int) x). But names create headaches in formal proofs: we need α-equivalence, capture-avoiding substitution, and freshness conditions. De Bruijn indices eliminate all of this by replacing names with numbers.

The idea: a variable is a natural number that counts how many binders you have to skip over to reach the one that binds it. Variable 0 refers to the nearest enclosing binder, 1 to the next one out, and so on:

Named:       (λ (x : int) (λ (y : bool) x))
De Bruijn:   (λ int (λ bool (var 1)))
                                  ↑
                          skip 1 binder (past y) to reach x

Named:       (λ (x : int) (λ (y : bool) y))
De Bruijn:   (λ int (λ bool (var 0)))
                                  ↑
                          skip 0 binders: nearest binder is y

Named:       (λ (f : int → int) (λ (x : int) (f x)))
De Bruijn:   (λ (int ⇒ int) (λ int (app (var 1) (var 0))))
                                          ↑          ↑
                                      f = skip 1   x = skip 0

The payoff: two terms that differ only in variable names (α-equivalent terms) get the exact same de Bruijn representation. We never need to rename variables, and substitution becomes a mechanical operation on indices.

QuickAnswer

Write (λ (x : int) (λ (y : int) (+ x y))) in de Bruijn notation. What index does x get? What about y?

Expressions and values

inductive Expr : Type where
  | var     : Nat → Expr
  | litInt  : Int → Expr
  | litBool : Bool → Expr
  | lam     : Ty → Expr → Expr
  | app     : Expr → Expr → Expr
  | add     : Expr → Expr → Expr
  | neg     : Expr → Expr
  | ifz     : Expr → Expr → Expr → Expr
  | letE    : Expr → Expr → Expr
  deriving Repr

inductive Value : Expr → Prop where
  | litInt  (n : Int)              : Value (.litInt n)
  | litBool (b : Bool)             : Value (.litBool b)
  | lam     (τ : Ty) (body : Expr) : Value (.lam τ body)

A note on the .foo syntax in Lean4. You’ll see .litInt, .lam, .app, etc. throughout this code. The dot prefix is Lean4’s shorthand for a constructor when the type can be inferred from context. Writing .litInt n is short for Expr.litInt n: Lean knows from the surrounding type that we’re building an Expr, so we can drop the Expr. prefix and just write .litInt. Similarly, .int is short for Ty.int. You’ll see this everywhere in Lean4 code: it keeps things concise without losing information, because the type checker always knows which type’s constructor you mean. If you see .foo, mentally read it as “the foo constructor of whatever type is expected here.”

Value is a proposition: Value e is a type that is inhabited exactly when e is a literal or a lambda. The constructors are proofs: Value.litInt 42 proves that .litInt 42 is a value.

Shifting and substitution

De Bruijn indices require two operations that named variables don’t.

Shifting (shift d c e): when we move a term under a new binder, its free variables need to be incremented so they still point to the right place. The cutoff c tracks how many binders we’ve entered, so bound variables (below c) are left alone:

Before shift:    (λ int (var 0) (var 1))
                              ↑          ↑
                          bound (0)   free (1)

After shift 1 0: (λ int (var 0) (var 2))
                              ↑          ↑
                        still bound   free, shifted up

Substitution (subst j s e): replace variable j with term s, and decrement variables above j (since the binder that introduced variable j has been consumed by β-reduction). Under a binder, j increments and s gets shifted:

def shift (d : Nat) (c : Nat) : Expr → Expr
  | .var k      => if k < c then .var k else .var (k + d)
  | .litInt n   => .litInt n
  | .litBool b  => .litBool b
  | .lam τ body => .lam τ (shift d (c + 1) body)
  | .app e₁ e₂  => .app (shift d c e₁) (shift d c e₂)
  | .add e₁ e₂  => .add (shift d c e₁) (shift d c e₂)
  | .neg e      => .neg (shift d c e)
  | .ifz e₁ e₂ e₃ => .ifz (shift d c e₁) (shift d c e₂) (shift d c e₃)
  | .letE e₁ e₂ => .letE (shift d c e₁) (shift d (c + 1) e₂)

def subst (j : Nat) (s : Expr) : Expr → Expr
  | .var k      => if k == j then s
                    else if j < k then .var (k - 1)
                    else .var k
  | .litInt n   => .litInt n
  | .litBool b  => .litBool b
  | .lam τ body => .lam τ (subst (j + 1) (shift 1 0 s) body)
  | .app e₁ e₂  => .app (subst j s e₁) (subst j s e₂)
  | .add e₁ e₂  => .add (subst j s e₁) (subst j s e₂)
  | .neg e      => .neg (subst j s e)
  | .ifz e₁ e₂ e₃ => .ifz (subst j s e₁) (subst j s e₂) (subst j s e₃)
  | .letE e₁ e₂ => .letE (subst j s e₁) (subst (j + 1) (shift 1 0 s) e₂)

Notice how subst under a lam increments j (the variable being replaced is one deeper) and shifts s (so its free variables still refer to the right things). This is the standard TAPL Chapter 6 formulation.

Typing contexts

A context maps de Bruijn indices to types. We represent it as a function Nat → Option Ty: position 0 is the most recent binder. extend pushes a new type at position 0. insertAt inserts at an arbitrary position (needed for the weakening lemma).

abbrev Ctx := Nat → Option Ty

def Ctx.empty : Ctx := fun _ => none

def Ctx.extend (Γ : Ctx) (τ : Ty) : Ctx
  | 0     => some τ
  | n + 1 => Γ n

def Ctx.insertAt (Γ : Ctx) (c : Nat) (τ : Ty) : Ctx :=
  fun n => if n < c then Γ n
           else if n = c then some τ
           else Γ (n - 1)

Using a function (rather than a list) makes context operations simple and avoids all list-index arithmetic.

The typing relation

Each constructor of HasType corresponds to one natural deduction typing rule from the STLC lecture. Here they are side by side: the mathematical rule on the left, its Lean4 encoding on the right. Everything above the inference line becomes a premise (an argument before the →); everything below the line becomes the conclusion (the return type).

Rule
Lean4 
| tInt (Γ : Ctx) (n : Int)
  : HasType Γ (.litInt n) .int
Rule
Lean4 
| tBool (Γ : Ctx) (b : Bool)
  : HasType Γ (.litBool b) .bool
Rule
where (x : τ) ∈ Γ
Lean4 
| tVar (Γ : Ctx) (i : Nat) (τ : Ty)
  (h : Γ i = some τ)
  : HasType Γ (.var i) τ
Rule
Lean4 
| tLam (Γ : Ctx) (τ₁ τ₂ : Ty)
  (body : Expr)
  : HasType (Γ.extend τ₁) body τ₂
  → HasType Γ (.lam τ₁ body) (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂)
Rule
Lean4 
| tApp (Γ : Ctx) (e₁ e₂ : Expr)
  (τ₁ τ₂ : Ty)
  : HasType Γ e₁ (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂)
  → HasType Γ e₂ τ₁
  → HasType Γ (.app e₁ e₂) τ₂
Rule
Lean4 
| tAdd (Γ : Ctx) (e₁ e₂ : Expr)
  : HasType Γ e₁ .int
  → HasType Γ e₂ .int
  → HasType Γ (.add e₁ e₂) .int
Rule
Lean4 
| tIf (Γ : Ctx) (e₁ e₂ e₃ : Expr)
  (τ : Ty)

  | appL    (e₁ e₁' e₂ : Expr)
    : Step e₁ e₁' → Step (.app e₁ e₂) (.app e₁' e₂)
  | appR    (v₁ e₂ e₂' : Expr)
    : Value v₁ → Step e₂ e₂' → Step (.app v₁ e₂) (.app v₁ e₂')
  | appAbs  (τ : Ty) (body v₂ : Expr)
    : Value v₂ → Step (.app (.lam τ body) v₂) (subst 0 v₂ body)
  | addL    (e₁ e₁' e₂ : Expr)
    : Step e₁ e₁' → Step (.add e₁ e₂) (.add e₁' e₂)
  | addR    (v₁ e₂ e₂' : Expr)
    : Value v₁ → Step e₂ e₂' → Step (.add v₁ e₂) (.add v₁ e₂')
  | addN    (n₁ n₂ : Int)
    : Step (.add (.litInt n₁) (.litInt n₂)) (.litInt (n₁ + n₂))
  | negStep (e e' : Expr)
    : Step e e' → Step (.neg e) (.neg e')
  | negN    (n : Int)
    : Step (.neg (.litInt n)) (.litInt (-n))
  | ifStep  (e₁ e₁' e₂ e₃ : Expr)
    : Step e₁ e₁' → Step (.ifz e₁ e₂ e₃) (.ifz e₁' e₂ e₃)
  | ifTrue  (e₂ e₃ : Expr)
    : Step (.ifz (.litInt 0) e₂ e₃) e₂
  | ifFalse (n : Int) (e₂ e₃ : Expr)
    : n ≠ 0 → Step (.ifz (.litInt n) e₂ e₃) e₃
  | letStep (e₁ e₁' e₂ : Expr)
    : Step e₁ e₁' → Step (.letE e₁ e₂) (.letE e₁' e₂)
  | letVal  (v₁ e₂ : Expr)
    : Value v₁ → Step (.letE v₁ e₂) (subst 0 v₁ e₂)

The pattern: congruence rules (appL, appR, addL, etc.) step inside a compound expression. Computation rules (appAbs, addN, ifTrue, etc.) do the actual work when all operands are values.

Canonical Forms

Before we tackle the main theorems, we need a small observation that will come up repeatedly. Think about what happens when we know something is a value with a specific type. There are only three kinds of values: integer literals, boolean literals, and lambdas. And each one can only have certain types:

  • An integer literal like 42 can only have type int (by T-Int).
  • A boolean literal can only have type bool (by T-Bool).
  • A lambda can only have an arrow type τ₁ → τ₂ (by T-Lam).

The canonical forms lemma just makes this official: if you know both the type and that something is a value, you know its exact shape.

Why do we care? Imagine you’re trying to prove progress for (e₁ e₂). You’ve established (via the IH) that e₁ is a value with type τ₁ → τ₂. You want to use E-AppAbs, but that rule requires e₁ to literally be (λ (x:τ₁) body). Canonical forms bridges the gap: “value with arrow type” implies “is a lambda.”

The proof is by cases on the value. Each impossible combination (e.g., litBool with type int) is a contradiction, which Lean resolves automatically with cases ht:

theorem canonical_int {Γ : Ctx} {e : Expr}
    (ht : HasType Γ e .int) (hv : Value e) :
    ∃ n : Int, e = .litInt n := by
  cases hv with
  | litInt n       => exact ⟨n, rfl⟩
  | litBool b      => cases ht
  | lam τ body     => cases ht

theorem canonical_bool {Γ : Ctx} {e : Expr}
    (ht : HasType Γ e .bool) (hv : Value e) :
    ∃ b : Bool, e = .litBool b := by
  cases hv with
  | litBool b      => exact ⟨b, rfl⟩
  | litInt n       => cases ht
  | lam τ body     => cases ht

theorem canonical_arrow {Γ : Ctx} {e : Expr} {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty}
    (ht : HasType Γ e (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂)) (hv : Value e) :
    ∃ body : Expr, e = .lam τ₁ body := by
  cases hv with
  | lam τ body =>
    cases ht with
    | tLam => exact ⟨body, rfl⟩
  | litInt n       => cases ht
  | litBool b      => cases ht

The ⟨n, rfl⟩ syntax is Lean’s way of providing an existential witness: “the witness is n, and the proof of equality is reflexivity.” The cases ht tactic asks Lean to find a typing rule that could assign the given type to the given value form; when none exists, the case is impossible and Lean closes it.

Progress

Theorem. If HasType Ctx.empty e τ (well-typed, closed), then either e is a value or there exists e' such that Step e e'.

How would you approach this proof?

The first question: what do we induct on? We have a well-typed expression e, so our options are: induction on e (the expression structure), or induction on the typing derivation (the proof that e has type τ). Let’s think about what each gives us.

If we induct on e, we’d case-split on whether e is a variable, a literal, a lambda, an application, etc. For a literal, we’re done (it’s a value). For an application (e₁ e₂), we’d know by IH that e₁ and e₂ satisfy progress… but wait, we only know they satisfy progress if they’re well-typed. The IH from structural induction on e doesn’t give us that. We’d have to extract the subderivations from the typing proof, which is awkward.

Induction on the typing derivation is cleaner. Each case of the induction corresponds to a typing rule (T-Int, T-App, T-Lam, etc.), and the IH gives us progress for the premises of that rule. For T-App, the IH directly says “e₁ satisfies progress” and “e₂ satisfies progress,” which is exactly what we need.

Lesson: when your theorem’s hypothesis is a derivation (like a typing proof), induct on the derivation.

Walking through a concrete example

Consider ((λ (x : int) x) 5) : int. Its typing derivation is:

The progress proof walks this tree bottom-up. We’re at the root, T-App, so we need to show the application can step. The IH tells us about the two children:

  • Left child (λ (x : int) x): typed by T-Lam, which is a value (lambdas are values). IH says: “it’s a value.” Good.
  • Right child 5: typed by T-Int, which is a value (literals are values). IH says: “it’s a value.” Good.

Both are values. Now what? We know e₁ has type int → int and is a value. By canonical forms, it must be a lambda. So e₁ = (λ τ body) for some body. Now E-AppAbs applies: ((λ τ body) 5) → subst 0 5 body. We found our step.

Now consider a different example: ((+ 3 5) 7). This is typed by T-App, where the left child is (+ 3 5) typed by T-Add. The IH on the left child says: both 3 and 5 are values (by T-Int), both are integers (by canonical forms), so E-AddN fires and (+ 3 5) → 8. Since the left child can step, E-AppL fires: ((+ 3 5) 7) → (8 7). We didn’t even need to look at the right child.

This is the general pattern for all compound cases:

  1. Ask the IH about each subexpression.
  2. If any subexpression can step, use the corresponding congruence rule (E-AppL, E-AppR, E-AddL, etc.).
  3. If all subexpressions are values, use canonical forms to determine their shapes, then identify the computation rule.

The proof, case by case

Values (T-Int, T-Bool, T-Lam): These are already values. Done immediately.

Variables (T-Var): The term is closed (empty context), so no variable can be in scope. The context lookup Γ i = some τ is impossible when Γ = Ctx.empty. Contradiction.

Application (T-App): The interesting case. We have ⊢ (e₁ e₂) : τ₂ with ⊢ e₁ : τ₁ → τ₂ and ⊢ e₂ : τ₁. The IH gives us progress for both children. Three subcases:

  • e₁ can step → use E-AppL: (e₁ e₂) → (e₁' e₂)
  • e₁ is a value, e₂ can step → use E-AppR: (v₁ e₂) → (v₁ e₂')
  • Both values → canonical forms on e₁ gives us a lambda → E-AppAbs

Addition (T-Add): Same pattern. If either operand steps, use E-AddL or E-AddR. If both are values, canonical forms gives us integer literals, so E-AddN fires.

Conditional (T-If): The condition e₁ has type int. If it steps, use E-IfStep. If it’s a value, canonical forms gives us an integer n. Then we decide: if n = 0, use E-IfTrue; otherwise E-IfFalse.

Let (T-Let): Simplest compound case. If e₁ steps, E-LetStep. If e₁ is a value, E-LetVal.

The full Lean4 proof

private theorem progress_aux (Γ : Ctx) (e : Expr) (τ : Ty)
    (ht : HasType Γ e τ) (hΓ : Γ = Ctx.empty) :
    Value e ∨ ∃ e' : Expr, Step e e' := by
  induction ht with
  | tInt  => left; exact Value.litInt _
  | tBool => left; exact Value.litBool _
  | tVar _ i _ h => subst hΓ; simp [Ctx.empty] at h
  | tLam => left; exact Value.lam _ _
  | tApp _ e₁ e₂ τ₁ τ₂ ht₁ ht₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    right
    rcases ih₁ hΓ with hv₁ | ⟨e₁', hs₁⟩
    · rcases ih₂ hΓ with hv₂ | ⟨e₂', hs₂⟩
      · obtain ⟨body, rfl⟩ := canonical_arrow ht₁ hv₁
        exact ⟨_, Step.appAbs _ _ _ hv₂⟩
      · exact ⟨_, Step.appR _ _ _ hv₁ hs₂⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.appL _ _ _ hs₁⟩
  | tAdd _ e₁ e₂ ht₁ ht₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    right
    rcases ih₁ hΓ with hv₁ | ⟨e₁', hs₁⟩
    · rcases ih₂ hΓ with hv₂ | ⟨e₂', hs₂⟩
      · obtain ⟨n₁, rfl⟩ := canonical_int ht₁ hv₁
        obtain ⟨n₂, rfl⟩ := canonical_int ht₂ hv₂
        exact ⟨_, Step.addN _ _⟩
      · exact ⟨_, Step.addR _ _ _ hv₁ hs₂⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.addL _ _ _ hs₁⟩
  | tNeg _ e ht ih =>
    right
    rcases ih hΓ with hv | ⟨e', hs⟩
    · obtain ⟨n, rfl⟩ := canonical_int ht hv
      exact ⟨_, Step.negN _⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.negStep _ _ hs⟩
  | tIf _ e₁ e₂ e₃ τ ht₁ _ _ ih₁ _ _ =>
    right
    rcases ih₁ hΓ with hv₁ | ⟨e₁', hs₁⟩
    · obtain ⟨n, rfl⟩ := canonical_int ht₁ hv₁
      by_cases h : n = 0
      · subst h; exact ⟨_, Step.ifTrue _ _⟩
      · exact ⟨_, Step.ifFalse _ _ _ h⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.ifStep _ _ _ _ hs₁⟩
  | tLet _ e₁ e₂ τ₁ τ₂ _ _ ih₁ _ =>
    right
    rcases ih₁ hΓ with hv₁ | ⟨e₁', hs₁⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.letVal _ _ hv₁⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.letStep _ _ _ hs₁⟩

theorem progress {e : Expr} {τ : Ty} (ht : HasType Ctx.empty e τ) :
    Value e ∨ ∃ e' : Expr, Step e e' :=
  progress_aux Ctx.empty e τ ht rfl

Reading the proof case by case:

  • tInt/tBool/tLam: already a value. left picks the first disjunct.
  • tVar: subst hΓ replaces the context with Ctx.empty, then simp [Ctx.empty] at h shows the lookup h is impossible (empty context maps everything to none).
  • tApp: right says we’ll find a step. rcases ih₁ hΓ splits the IH on e₁ into “value” or “steps.” If e₁ steps, use appL. If e₁ is a value, split the IH on e₂. If both are values, canonical_arrow tells us e₁ is a lambda, so appAbs fires.
  • tAdd: same pattern, but canonical_int extracts literal integers, so addN fires.
  • tIf: after canonical forms gives us an integer, by_cases h : n = 0 decides which branch.
  • tLet: simplest compound case: if e₁ is a value, letVal; if it steps, letStep.

The Substitution Lemma

This is the hardest proof in the development, and the most important one to understand deeply. Let’s build it from scratch, starting with why we need it and discovering the complications as we go.

Why we need this lemma

When β-reduction fires, (λ body) v → body[0 := v], we need to know the result is still well-typed. We have:

  • Γ.extend τ₁ ⊢ body : τ₂ (the body is typed with variable 0 bound to τ₁)
  • Γ ⊢ v : τ₁ (the argument has the right type)

We need: Γ ⊢ body[0 := v] : τ₂. Intuitively this should work: every place body used variable 0, it expected a τ₁, and v is a τ₁. But “intuitively should work” isn’t a proof. Let’s try.

First attempt: induction at position 0

We try to prove: if Γ.extend τ₁ ⊢ e : τ₂ and Γ ⊢ v : τ₁, then Γ ⊢ subst 0 v e : τ₂. We induct on the typing derivation of e.

T-Var case, variable is 0: The substitution replaces variable 0 with v. We need Γ ⊢ v : τ₁. That’s exactly our hypothesis.

T-Var case, variable is i > 0: The substitution decrements i to i-1. We need Γ (i-1) = some τ. Since the original lookup was (Γ.extend τ₁) i = some τ, and i > 0, this is Γ (i-1). Works.

T-App case: Structural, apply IH to both subexpressions. Fine.

T-Lam case: here’s where we get stuck. We have a nested lambda: (λ σ body') typed under Γ.extend τ₁. The premise is:

(Γ.extend τ₁).extend σ ⊢ body' : τ₂'

After substitution, subst 0 v (λ σ body') becomes λ σ (subst 1 (shift 1 0 v) body'). So we need:

Γ.extend σ ⊢ subst 1 (shift 1 0 v) body' : τ₂'

But our IH only talks about substitution at position 0! We need position 1 here. The IH doesn’t apply.

The fix: generalize over the position

The failed attempt reveals what we need: a lemma that works at any substitution position j, not just 0. Under each binder, j increments. The generalized statement:

If Γ.insertAt j τ₁ ⊢ e : τ₂ and Γ ⊢ v : τ₁, then Γ ⊢ subst j v e : τ₂.

Now in the T-Lam case, the IH gives us substitution at position j+1, which is exactly what we need after going under the binder.

But we hit another wall: weakening

In the T-Lam case with the generalized lemma, we have Γ ⊢ v : τ₁ and we need Γ.extend σ ⊢ shift 1 0 v : τ₁ (because v gets shifted when it goes under the new binder). This is a weakening lemma: adding a type to the context (and shifting accordingly) preserves typing.

Weakening is itself proved by induction on the typing derivation. The interesting case is T-Lam, which uses a commutation lemma: extending a context and then inserting at position c is the same as inserting at position c+1 and then extending. This is the key piece of de Bruijn bookkeeping.

So the full dependency chain is:

commutation (extend_insertAt)
    ↓
weakening
    ↓
substitution (generalized)
    ↓
substitution (at position 0)

Each lemma was discovered by getting stuck in the proof of the next one. This is typical of formalization: the proof attempt itself tells you what lemmas you need.

Lean4 code: building up the infrastructure

Context helper lemmas (properties of insertAt):

These are the basic facts about inserting into a context. They say: looking up the inserted position gives the inserted type; below is unchanged; above is shifted down. We’ll use these throughout.

theorem Ctx.insertAt_self (Γ : Ctx) (j : Nat) (σ : Ty) :
    (Γ.insertAt j σ) j = some σ := by
  simp [Ctx.insertAt]

theorem Ctx.insertAt_lt (Γ : Ctx) (j i : Nat) (σ : Ty) (h : i < j) :
    (Γ.insertAt j σ) i = Γ i := by
  simp [Ctx.insertAt, h]

theorem Ctx.insertAt_gt (Γ : Ctx) (j i : Nat) (σ : Ty) (h : j < i) :
    (Γ.insertAt j σ) i = Γ (i - 1) := by
  unfold Ctx.insertAt
  have h1 : ¬(i < j) := by omega
  have h2 : ¬(i = j) := by omega
  rw [if_neg h1, if_neg h2]

theorem Ctx.insertAt_zero (Γ : Ctx) (σ : Ty) :
    Γ.insertAt 0 σ = Γ.extend σ := by
  funext n; simp [Ctx.insertAt, Ctx.extend]; cases n <;> simp

Weakening (the lemma we discovered was needed in the T-Lam case):

The key case is T-Lam, which uses the commutation lemma extend_insertAt. The rest are structural.

theorem weakening {Γ : Ctx} {e : Expr} {τ σ : Ty} {c : Nat}
    (ht : HasType Γ e τ) :
    HasType (Γ.insertAt c σ) (shift 1 c e) τ := by
  induction ht generalizing c with
  | tInt _ n => simp [shift]; exact HasType.tInt _ _
  | tBool _ b => simp [shift]; exact HasType.tBool _ _
  | tVar _ i τ hlookup =>
    simp only [shift]
    split
    · next hlt =>
      exact HasType.tVar _ _ _
        (by rw [Ctx.insertAt_lt _ c _ σ hlt]; exact hlookup)
    · next hge =>
      have hge' : c ≤ i := Nat.le_of_not_lt hge
      have hgt : c < i + 1 := by omega
      apply HasType.tVar
      rw [Ctx.insertAt_gt _ c _ σ hgt]
      have : i + 1 - 1 = i := by omega
      rw [this]; exact hlookup
  | tLam _ τ₁ τ₂ body _ ih =>
    simp [shift]
    apply HasType.tLam
    rw [← Ctx.extend_insertAt]
    exact ih
  | tApp _ e₁ e₂ τ₁ τ₂ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    simp [shift]; exact HasType.tApp _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂
  | tAdd _ e₁ e₂ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    simp [shift]; exact HasType.tAdd _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂
  | tNeg _ e _ ih =>
    simp [shift]; exact HasType.tNeg _ _ ih
  | tIf _ e₁ e₂ e₃ τ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
    simp [shift]; exact HasType.tIf _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃
  | tLet _ e₁ e₂ τ₁ τ₂ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    simp [shift]
    apply HasType.tLet _ _ _ _ _
    · exact ih₁
    · rw [← Ctx.extend_insertAt]; exact ih₂

The T-Var case splits on whether the variable is below or above the insertion point. The T-Lam case uses Ctx.extend_insertAt: extending a context and then inserting is the same as inserting and then extending (with the position shifted). This commutation lemma is the key piece of de Bruijn bookkeeping.

Generalized substitution (at arbitrary position j):

private theorem subst_aux (Γ₀ : Ctx) (e : Expr) (τ₂ : Ty)
    (he : HasType Γ₀ e τ₂)
    (Γ : Ctx) (v : Expr) (τ₁ : Ty) (j : Nat)
    (hΓ : Γ₀ = Γ.insertAt j τ₁) (hv : HasType Γ v τ₁) :
    HasType Γ (subst j v e) τ₂ := by
  induction he generalizing Γ j v τ₁ with
  | tInt => subst hΓ; simp [subst]; exact HasType.tInt _ _
  | tBool => subst hΓ; simp [subst]; exact HasType.tBool _ _
  | tVar _ i τ hlookup =>
    subst hΓ; simp [subst]
    split
    · next heq =>
      have hij : i = j := by omega
      subst hij
      rw [Ctx.insertAt_self] at hlookup
      injection hlookup with h; subst h; exact hv
    · split
      · next hne hjlt =>
        have hij : j < i := by omega
        rw [Ctx.insertAt_gt _ _ _ _ hij] at hlookup
        exact HasType.tVar _ _ _ hlookup
      · next hne hjge =>
        have hij : i < j := by omega
        rw [Ctx.insertAt_lt _ _ _ _ hij] at hlookup
        exact HasType.tVar _ _ _ hlookup
  | tLam _ τ₁' τ₂' body _ ih =>
    subst hΓ; simp [subst]
    apply HasType.tLam
    apply ih
    · exact (Ctx.extend_insertAt Γ τ₁' τ₁ j).symm
    · have h := @weakening Γ _ _ τ₁' 0 hv
      rwa [Ctx.insertAt_zero] at h
  | tApp _ e₁ e₂ σ₁ σ₂ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    subst hΓ; simp [subst]
    exact HasType.tApp _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ _ _ _ rfl hv) (ih₂ _ _ _ _ rfl hv)
  | tAdd _ e₁ e₂ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    subst hΓ; simp [subst]
    exact HasType.tAdd _ _ _ (ih₁ _ _ _ _ rfl hv) (ih₂ _ _ _ _ rfl hv)
  | tNeg _ e _ ih =>
    subst hΓ; simp [subst]
    exact HasType.tNeg _ _ (ih _ _ _ _ rfl hv)
  | tIf _ e₁ e₂ e₃ τ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
    subst hΓ; simp [subst]
    exact HasType.tIf _ _ _ _ _
      (ih₁ _ _ _ _ rfl hv) (ih₂ _ _ _ _ rfl hv) (ih₃ _ _ _ _ rfl hv)
  | tLet _ e₁ e₂ σ₁ σ₂ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    subst hΓ; simp [subst]
    apply HasType.tLet _ _ _ _ _
    · exact ih₁ _ _ _ _ rfl hv
    · apply ih₂
      · exact (Ctx.extend_insertAt Γ σ₁ τ₁ j).symm
      · have h := @weakening Γ _ _ σ₁ 0 hv
        rwa [Ctx.insertAt_zero] at h

Reading the key cases:

  • tVar (i = j): the variable being substituted. insertAt_self tells us the looked-up type is τ₁. Since the substitution replaces it with v, and v has type τ₁, we’re done.
  • tVar (i > j): above the substitution point. The index decrements by one (since a binder was consumed). insertAt_gt aligns the context lookup.
  • tVar (i < j): below the substitution point. Unchanged. insertAt_lt aligns.
  • tLam: the induction increments j and shifts v. We need the commutation lemma (extend_insertAt) to align the context, and weakening at position 0 to give v the right type under the extended context.
  • All other cases: structural. Apply IH to each subexpression, passing rfl for the context equation and hv for the value typing.

The public API wraps this at position 0:

theorem substitution_general {Γ : Ctx} {e v : Expr} {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty}
    {j : Nat}
    (he : HasType (Γ.insertAt j τ₁) e τ₂) (hv : HasType Γ v τ₁) :
    HasType Γ (subst j v e) τ₂ :=

theorem substitution {Γ : Ctx} {e v : Expr} {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty}
    (he : HasType (Γ.extend τ₁) e τ₂)
    (hv : HasType Γ v τ₁) :
    HasType Γ (subst 0 v e) τ₂ := by
  rw [Ctx.extend_eq_insertAt] at he
  exact substitution_general he hv

QuickAnswer

In the T-Var case when i = j, what tells us that τ = τ₁ (the type of the variable equals the type of the substituted value)?

Preservation

Theorem. If HasType Γ e τ and Step e e', then HasType Γ e' τ.

How would you approach this proof?

Again, what do we induct on? We have two things: a typing derivation ht : HasType Γ e τ and a step hs : Step e e'. We could try induction on hs (the step), but then we’d need to extract typing information for the subexpressions, which is awkward. Induction on ht (the typing) works better: each case tells us the shape of e, and then we do case analysis on which step rule could have fired.

Most cases fall into two patterns:

Congruence cases (e.g., T-App + E-AppL): a subexpression stepped. The IH says it preserved its type. Rebuild the typing derivation with the new subexpression. This is mechanical.

Computation cases (e.g., T-App + E-AppAbs): the real work. β-reduction produces subst 0 v₂ body. We need to show this is well-typed. This is exactly what the substitution lemma says. The entire substitution infrastructure we just built exists for this single moment.

Walking through β-reduction concretely

Take ((λ (x : int) (+ x 1)) 5) → (+ 5 1). The typing derivation before the step:

E-AppAbs fires. From the derivation, we extract:

  • x : int ⊢ (+ x 1) : int (the body is well-typed assuming x is int)
  • ⊢ 5 : int (the argument is an int)

The substitution lemma says: since the body is typed under Γ.extend int and 5 has type int under Γ, then subst 0 5 (+ x 1) (which is (+ 5 1)) has type int under Γ. That’s preservation for this step.

After the step, the derivation of (+ 5 1) : int is:

The substitution lemma constructed this derivation for us: it walked through the body (+ x 1), replaced the T-Var node for x with the T-Int proof for 5, and rebuilt the T-Add on top.

QuickAnswer

What happens in the T-App + E-AppL case (function position steps)? Why is this case easier than β-reduction?

The full Lean4 proof

private theorem preservation_general {Γ : Ctx} {e e' : Expr} {τ : Ty}
    (ht : HasType Γ e τ) (hs : Step e e') :
    HasType Γ e' τ := by
  induction ht generalizing e' with
  | tInt => cases hs
  | tBool => cases hs
  | tVar => cases hs
  | tLam => cases hs
  | tApp Γ e₁ e₂ τ₁ τ₂ ht₁ ht₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    cases hs with
    | appL _ e₁' _ hs₁ =>
      exact HasType.tApp _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ hs₁) ht₂
    | appR _ _ e₂' _ hs₂ =>
      exact HasType.tApp _ _ _ _ _ ht₁ (ih₂ hs₂)
    | appAbs _ body _ hv₂ =>
      cases ht₁ with
      | tLam _ _ _ _ htbody => exact substitution htbody ht₂
  | tAdd Γ e₁ e₂ ht₁ ht₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    cases hs with
    | addL _ e₁' _ hs₁ =>
      exact HasType.tAdd _ _ _ (ih₁ hs₁) ht₂
    | addR _ _ e₂' _ hs₂ =>
      exact HasType.tAdd _ _ _ ht₁ (ih₂ hs₂)
    | addN => exact HasType.tInt _ _
  | tNeg Γ e ht ih =>
    cases hs with
    | negStep _ e' hs' => exact HasType.tNeg _ _ (ih hs')
    | negN => exact HasType.tInt _ _
  | tIf Γ e₁ e₂ e₃ τ ht₁ ht₂ ht₃ ih₁ _ _ =>
    cases hs with
    | ifStep _ e₁' _ _ hs₁ =>
      exact HasType.tIf _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ hs₁) ht₂ ht₃
    | ifTrue => exact ht₂
    | ifFalse => exact ht₃
  | tLet Γ e₁ e₂ τ₁ τ₂ ht₁ ht₂ ih₁ _ =>
    cases hs with
    | letStep _ e₁' _ hs₁ =>
      exact HasType.tLet _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ hs₁) ht₂
    | letVal _ _ hv₁ => exact substitution ht₂ ht₁

theorem preservation {e e' : Expr} {τ : Ty}
    (ht : HasType Ctx.empty e τ) (hs : Step e e') :
    HasType Ctx.empty e' τ :=
  preservation_general ht hs

Reading the key cases:

  • tInt/tBool/tVar/tLam: these forms can never step (cases hs finds no matching step rule), so the cases are vacuously true.
  • tApp + appAbs: this is β-reduction, the critical case. We invert ht₁ to extract htbody : HasType (Γ.extend τ₁) body τ₂, then apply substitution htbody ht₂ to conclude that subst 0 v₂ body has type τ₂.
  • tApp + appL/appR: congruence. The subexpression that stepped preserves its type by IH; rebuild with tApp.
  • tAdd + addN: both operands were integer literals, so the result litInt (n₁ + n₂) has type int by tInt.
  • tIf + ifTrue/ifFalse: the selected branch already has the right type (both branches were required to have type τ by tIf).
  • tLet + letVal: same as β-reduction: apply substitution.

QuickAnswer

In the tApp + appAbs case, what would go wrong if we didn’t have the substitution lemma? What would we be unable to conclude?

Putting It Together: Type Soundness

With progress and preservation in hand, type soundness follows by iteration:

inductive MultiStep : Expr → Expr → Prop where
  | refl (e : Expr) : MultiStep e e
  | step (e e' e'' : Expr)
    : Step e e' → MultiStep e' e'' → MultiStep e e''

theorem preservation_multi {e e' : Expr} {τ : Ty}
    (ht : HasType Ctx.empty e τ) (hms : MultiStep e e') :
    HasType Ctx.empty e' τ := by
  induction hms with
  | refl => exact ht
  | step _ _ _ hs _ ih => exact ih (preservation ht hs)

theorem type_soundness {e e' : Expr} {τ : Ty}
    (ht : HasType Ctx.empty e τ) (hms : MultiStep e e') :
    Value e' ∨ ∃ e'' : Expr, Step e' e'' :=
  progress (preservation_multi ht hms)

MultiStep is the reflexive-transitive closure of Step. preservation_multi iterates preservation over multiple steps. type_soundness combines them: after any number of steps from a well-typed term, apply progress to the (still well-typed) result.

What this means: if you write a well-typed STLC program, you will never see a runtime type error. Every intermediate state is well-typed, and the program either keeps running or reaches a value. Since STLC has no general recursion (the Y combinator is untypable), every well-typed STLC program terminates and produces a value.

QuickAnswer

Why does STLC type soundness also imply termination? What feature would we need to add to STLC to get non-terminating programs?

The Lean4 Formalization

The complete Lean4 formalization lives in lecture-projects/stlc-lean/ in the course repository. To build it:

cd lecture-projects/stlc-lean && lake build
File What it formalizes
Syntax.lean Types, expressions, values, de Bruijn shifting, substitution, contexts
Typing.lean The typing relation HasType Γ e τ
Semantics.lean Small-step CBV operational semantics
CanonicalForms.lean Values match their types
Substitution.lean Weakening and the substitution lemma
Progress.lean Well-typed closed terms are not stuck
Preservation.lean Stepping preserves types; type soundness corollary

Every theorem is fully proved with zero sorry. The substitution proof required a generalized weakening lemma (insertAt at an arbitrary position) and a commutation lemma showing that extending a context commutes with insertion. These are the standard de Bruijn bookkeeping lemmas; they are mechanical but must be done carefully to get the index arithmetic right.

Summary

Concept Statement Intuition
Stuck Not a value, can’t step Runtime type error
Progress Well-typed closed → value or can step “You can always move”
Canonical forms Values have the shape their type predicts Ints are ints, functions are lambdas
Substitution lemma Plugging in a well-typed term preserves typing The heart of β-reduction safety
Preservation Stepping preserves the type “You stay on track”
Type soundness Progress + preservation, iterated Well-typed programs don’t go wrong

See also: Dependent De Bruijn Indices and Intrinsic Typing redoes this entire development with dependent de Bruijn indices, where the term type itself carries the typing proof. Preservation becomes free, and the formalization shrinks by half.

item.title: Dependent De Bruijn Indices and Intrinsic Typing
item.description:
Prerequisites: the STLC lecture and the type soundness notes.

In the type soundness notes, we proved progress and preservation for STLC the hard way. We defined untyped expressions, a separate typing relation, substitution with de Bruijn index arithmetic, a weakening lemma, a commutation lemma, and then proved progress and preservation. It was about 400 lines of Lean4, and the substitution infrastructure alone was 130 lines.

What if we could get the same guarantee with a fraction of the work?

The idea: instead of defining expressions and then proving they’re well-typed, we define expressions that are well-typed by construction. The de Bruijn indices become dependent: the term type is indexed by its typing context and its type. A Term Γ τ is, by construction, a well-typed term of type τ in context Γ. If you can build the term, it’s well-typed. If it’s ill-typed, you can’t build it.

This is sometimes called intrinsic typing, and it’s one of the deepest ideas in programming language theory. The principle extends far beyond type soundness: encoding invariants into your data structures eliminates the need to prove those invariants hold. Rust’s borrow checker, Haskell’s GADTs, and dependent types in Agda/Lean all use this idea.

What Changes?

In the extrinsic approach (the type soundness notes), we had two separate things:

-- The term (untyped data)
Expr : Type

-- The typing judgement (a separate proof)
HasType : Ctx → Expr → Ty → Prop

A term exists independently of its type. You construct the term, then separately prove it has a type. In the dependent de Bruijn approach, we fuse them:

-- The term IS the typing proof
Term : Ctx → Ty → Type

A Term Γ τ is simultaneously a term and a proof that it has type τ in context Γ. There’s no such thing as an ill-typed term.

QuickAnswer

In the extrinsic approach, what happens if you construct Expr.app (Expr.litInt 5) (Expr.litInt 3)? Is it well-typed? In the dependent de Bruijn approach, can you construct the analogous term?

The Full Lean4 Development

Types and contexts

Types are the same as before. A context is a list of types (de Bruijn: head is the most recent binder):

inductive Ty : Type where
  | int  : Ty
  | bool : Ty
  | arrow : Ty → Ty → Ty
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

abbrev Ctx := List Ty

Variables as membership proofs

In the extrinsic version, a variable was a Nat (de Bruijn index) plus a separate proof that the context maps it to the right type. With dependent de Bruijn, the variable is the proof: Mem τ Γ is a constructive proof that type τ appears in context Γ.

inductive Mem : Ty → Ctx → Type where
  | here  : {Γ : Ctx} → {τ : Ty} → Mem τ (τ :: Γ)
  | there : {Γ : Ctx} → {τ σ : Ty} → Mem τ Γ → Mem τ (σ :: Γ)

Mem.here says “I’m variable 0 and my type matches the head of the context.” Mem.there m says “skip one binder and use proof m for the rest.” For example, in context [int, bool, int]:

  • Mem.here : variable 0 has type int
  • Mem.there Mem.here : variable 1 has type bool
  • Mem.there (Mem.there Mem.here) : variable 2 has type int

There’s no way to construct a Mem .bool [.int, .int]: bool isn’t in [int, int]. Out-of-scope and mistyped variable references are unrepresentable.

Intrinsically-typed terms

Each constructor enforces its typing rule. Compare with the extrinsic version side by side:

Extrinsic (HasType) 
| tLam (Γ : Ctx) (τ₁ τ₂ : Ty)
  (body : Expr)
  : HasType (Γ.extend τ₁) body τ₂
  → HasType Γ (.lam τ₁ body) (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂)
Dependent de Bruijn 
| lam : Term (τ₁ :: Γ) τ₂
      → Term Γ (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂)
Extrinsic (HasType) 
| tApp (Γ : Ctx) (e₁ e₂ : Expr)
  (τ₁ τ₂ : Ty)
  : HasType Γ e₁ (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂)
  → HasType Γ e₂ τ₁
  → HasType Γ (.app e₁ e₂) τ₂
Dependent de Bruijn 
| app : Term Γ (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂)
      → Term Γ τ₁
      → Term Γ τ₂

Look at app. The extrinsic version takes two expressions plus two typing proofs. The dependent version takes two typed terms: the function must have type τ₁ ⇒ τ₂ and the argument must have type τ₁. If you try to pass a Term Γ .bool as the function, Lean rejects it: .bool doesn’t unify with τ₁ ⇒ τ₂.

The full definition:

inductive Term : Ctx → Ty → Type where
  | var     : {Γ : Ctx} → {τ : Ty} → Mem τ Γ → Term Γ τ
  | litInt  : {Γ : Ctx} → Int → Term Γ .int
  | litBool : {Γ : Ctx} → Bool → Term Γ .bool
  | lam     : {Γ : Ctx} → {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty} → Term (τ₁ :: Γ) τ₂ → Term Γ (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂)
  | app     : {Γ : Ctx} → {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty} → Term Γ (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂) → Term Γ τ₁ → Term Γ τ₂
  | add     : {Γ : Ctx} → Term Γ .int → Term Γ .int → Term Γ .int
  | neg     : {Γ : Ctx} → Term Γ .int → Term Γ .int
  | ifz     : {Γ : Ctx} → {τ : Ty} → Term Γ .int → Term Γ τ → Term Γ τ → Term Γ τ
  | letE    : {Γ : Ctx} → {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty} → Term Γ τ₁ → Term (τ₁ :: Γ) τ₂ → Term Γ τ₂

inductive Value : {Γ : Ctx} → {τ : Ty} → Term Γ τ → Prop where
  | litInt  {Γ : Ctx} (n : Int)                                    : Value (Γ := Γ) (.litInt n)
  | litBool {Γ : Ctx} (b : Bool)                                   : Value (Γ := Γ) (.litBool b)
  | lam     {Γ : Ctx} {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty} (body : Term (τ₁ :: Γ) τ₂)   : Value (.lam body)

Renaming and weakening

In the extrinsic version, shifting (adjusting de Bruijn indices when moving under a binder) was a function on raw Nat indices, and we needed a weakening theorem (30+ lines) to show it preserved typing. With dependent de Bruijn, renaming is a typed function. A Ren Γ Δ maps variables in Γ to variables in Δ, preserving types. Weakening falls out as a one-liner:

abbrev Ren (Γ Δ : Ctx) := {τ : Ty} → Mem τ Γ → Mem τ Δ

def Ren.ext {Γ Δ : Ctx} {τ : Ty} (ρ : Ren Γ Δ) : Ren (τ :: Γ) (τ :: Δ) :=
  fun {σ} m => match m with
  | .here => .here
  | .there m' => .there (ρ m')

def rename {Γ Δ : Ctx} {τ : Ty} (ρ : Ren Γ Δ) : Term Γ τ → Term Δ τ
  | .var m        => .var (ρ m)
  | .litInt n     => .litInt n
  | .litBool b    => .litBool b
  | .lam body     => .lam (rename ρ.ext body)
  | .app e₁ e₂    => .app (rename ρ e₁) (rename ρ e₂)
  | .add e₁ e₂    => .add (rename ρ e₁) (rename ρ e₂)
  | .neg e        => .neg (rename ρ e)
  | .ifz e₁ e₂ e₃ => .ifz (rename ρ e₁) (rename ρ e₂) (rename ρ e₃)
  | .letE e₁ e₂   => .letE (rename ρ e₁) (rename ρ.ext e₂)

def weaken {Γ : Ctx} {τ σ : Ty} : Term Γ τ → Term (σ :: Γ) τ :=
  rename (fun m => .there m)

Compare weaken here (one line, no proof) with the 30-line weakening theorem in the extrinsic version.

Typed substitution

A Sub Γ Δ maps variables in Γ to terms in Δ. Again, the types are preserved by construction:

abbrev Sub (Γ Δ : Ctx) := {τ : Ty} → Mem τ Γ → Term Δ τ

def Sub.ext {Γ Δ : Ctx} {τ : Ty} (σs : Sub Γ Δ) : Sub (τ :: Γ) (τ :: Δ) :=
  fun {ρ} m => match m with
  | .here => .var .here
  | .there m' => weaken (σs m')

def subst {Γ Δ : Ctx} {τ : Ty} (σs : Sub Γ Δ) : Term Γ τ → Term Δ τ
  | .var m        => σs m
  | .litInt n     => .litInt n
  | .litBool b    => .litBool b
  | .lam body     => .lam (subst σs.ext body)
  | .app e₁ e₂    => .app (subst σs e₁) (subst σs e₂)
  | .add e₁ e₂    => .add (subst σs e₁) (subst σs e₂)
  | .neg e        => .neg (subst σs e)
  | .ifz e₁ e₂ e₃ => .ifz (subst σs e₁) (subst σs e₂) (subst σs e₃)
  | .letE e₁ e₂   => .letE (subst σs e₁) (subst σs.ext e₂)

def substSingle {Γ : Ctx} {τ₁ : Ty} (v : Term Γ τ₁) : Sub (τ₁ :: Γ) Γ :=
  fun {τ} m =>
    match τ, m with
    | _, .here     => v
    | _, .there m' => .var m'

def substTop {Γ : Ctx} {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty} (v : Term Γ τ₁) (body : Term (τ₁ :: Γ) τ₂) : Term Γ τ₂ :=
  subst (substSingle v) body

Look at substTop’s type: it takes v : Term Γ τ₁ and body : Term (τ₁ :: Γ) τ₂ and returns Term Γ τ₂. The substitution lemma from the extrinsic version (130 lines of proof) is now the type signature of a function. No commutation lemma, no insertAt, no generalization over position. The types do all the work.

QuickAnswer

Why doesn’t the dependent de Bruijn version need a commutation lemma (extend_insertAt) for substitution under binders?

Small-step semantics: preservation is the signature

The critical difference:

-- Extrinsic: preservation is a THEOREM
Step : Expr → Expr → Prop
preservation : HasType Γ e τ → Step e e' → HasType Γ e' τ  -- 40 lines

-- Dependent de Bruijn: preservation is the TYPE SIGNATURE
Step : Term Γ τ → Term Γ τ → Prop
-- Both sides have the same Γ and τ. Nothing to prove.

The full step relation:

inductive Step : {Γ : Ctx} → {τ : Ty} → Term Γ τ → Term Γ τ → Prop where
  | appL     {Γ : Ctx} {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty} {e₁ e₁' : Term Γ (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂)} {e₂ : Term Γ τ₁}
             : Step e₁ e₁' → Step (.app e₁ e₂) (.app e₁' e₂)
  | appR     {Γ : Ctx} {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty} {v₁ : Term Γ (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂)} {e₂ e₂' : Term Γ τ₁}
             : Value v₁ → Step e₂ e₂' → Step (.app v₁ e₂) (.app v₁ e₂')
  | appAbs   {Γ : Ctx} {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty} {body : Term (τ₁ :: Γ) τ₂} {v₂ : Term Γ τ₁}
             : Value v₂ → Step (.app (.lam body) v₂) (substTop v₂ body)
  | addL     {Γ : Ctx} {e₁ e₁' e₂ : Term Γ .int}
             : Step e₁ e₁' → Step (.add e₁ e₂) (.add e₁' e₂)
  | addR     {Γ : Ctx} {v₁ e₂ e₂' : Term Γ .int}
             : Value v₁ → Step e₂ e₂' → Step (.add v₁ e₂) (.add v₁ e₂')
  | addN     {Γ : Ctx} {n₁ n₂ : Int}
             : Step (.add (.litInt n₁) (.litInt n₂)) (.litInt (n₁ + n₂) : Term Γ .int)
  | negStep  {Γ : Ctx} {e e' : Term Γ .int}
             : Step e e' → Step (.neg e) (.neg e')
  | negN     {Γ : Ctx} {n : Int}
             : Step (.neg (.litInt n)) (.litInt (-n) : Term Γ .int)
  | ifStep   {Γ : Ctx} {τ : Ty} {e₁ e₁' : Term Γ .int} {e₂ e₃ : Term Γ τ}
             : Step e₁ e₁' → Step (.ifz e₁ e₂ e₃) (.ifz e₁' e₂ e₃)
  | ifTrue   {Γ : Ctx} {τ : Ty} {e₂ e₃ : Term Γ τ}
             : Step (.ifz (.litInt 0) e₂ e₃) e₂
  | ifFalse  {Γ : Ctx} {τ : Ty} {n : Int} {e₂ e₃ : Term Γ τ}
             : n ≠ 0 → Step (.ifz (.litInt n) e₂ e₃) e₃
  | letStep  {Γ : Ctx} {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty} {e₁ e₁' : Term Γ τ₁} {e₂ : Term (τ₁ :: Γ) τ₂}
             : Step e₁ e₁' → Step (.letE e₁ e₂) (.letE e₁' e₂)
  | letVal   {Γ : Ctx} {τ₁ τ₂ : Ty} {v₁ : Term Γ τ₁} {e₂ : Term (τ₁ :: Γ) τ₂}
             : Value v₁ → Step (.letE v₁ e₂) (substTop v₁ e₂)

Progress

Progress still needs a proof (it’s about behavior, not types), but canonical forms is gone. When e₁ : Term [] (τ₁ ⇒ τ₂) is a value, pattern matching on Value e₁ directly gives Value.lam body: no other value constructor produces an arrow type. The type index does the work that the canonical forms lemma used to do.

theorem progress {τ : Ty} (t : Term [] τ) :
    Value t ∨ ∃ t' : Term [] τ, Step t t' := by
  match t with
  | .var m => exact (nomatch m)
  | .litInt _  => left; exact Value.litInt _
  | .litBool _ => left; exact Value.litBool _
  | .lam _     => left; exact Value.lam _
  | .app e₁ e₂ =>
    right
    have ih₁ := progress e₁
    have ih₂ := progress e₂
    rcases ih₁ with hv₁ | ⟨e₁', hs₁⟩
    · rcases ih₂ with hv₂ | ⟨e₂', hs₂⟩
      · cases hv₁ with
        | lam body => exact ⟨_, Step.appAbs hv₂⟩
      · exact ⟨_, Step.appR hv₁ hs₂⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.appL hs₁⟩
  | .add e₁ e₂ =>
    right
    have ih₁ := progress e₁
    have ih₂ := progress e₂
    rcases ih₁ with hv₁ | ⟨e₁', hs₁⟩
    · rcases ih₂ with hv₂ | ⟨e₂', hs₂⟩
      · cases hv₁ with
        | litInt n₁ => cases hv₂ with
          | litInt n₂ => exact ⟨_, Step.addN⟩
      · exact ⟨_, Step.addR hv₁ hs₂⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.addL hs₁⟩
  | .neg e =>
    right
    have ih := progress e
    rcases ih with hv | ⟨e', hs⟩
    · cases hv with
      | litInt n => exact ⟨_, Step.negN⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.negStep hs⟩
  | .ifz e₁ e₂ e₃ =>
    right
    have ih₁ := progress e₁
    rcases ih₁ with hv₁ | ⟨e₁', hs₁⟩
    · cases hv₁ with
      | litInt n =>
        by_cases h : n = 0
        · subst h; exact ⟨_, Step.ifTrue⟩
        · exact ⟨_, Step.ifFalse h⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.ifStep hs₁⟩
  | .letE e₁ e₂ =>
    right
    have ih₁ := progress e₁
    rcases ih₁ with hv₁ | ⟨e₁', hs₁⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.letVal hv₁⟩
    · exact ⟨_, Step.letStep hs₁⟩

Notice: the .app case does cases hv₁ with | lam body => ... directly. No canonical forms lemma needed. The type index τ₁ ⇒ τ₂ forces the only possible value constructor to be lam.

Type soundness

Preservation is free. Type soundness is just progress applied after multi-step:

inductive MultiStep : {Γ : Ctx} → {τ : Ty} → Term Γ τ → Term Γ τ → Prop where
  | refl  {Γ : Ctx} {τ : Ty} {t : Term Γ τ} : MultiStep t t
  | step  {Γ : Ctx} {τ : Ty} {t t' t'' : Term Γ τ}
          : Step t t' → MultiStep t' t'' → MultiStep t t''

theorem type_soundness {τ : Ty} (t : Term [] τ) {t' : Term [] τ}
    (hms : MultiStep t t') :
    Value t' ∨ ∃ t'' : Term [] τ, Step t' t'' :=
  progress t'

That’s it. One line. Preservation doesn’t appear because it was never needed: Step already guarantees the type is preserved by its signature.

The Comparison

  Extrinsic Dependent de Bruijn
Terms Expr : Type (untyped) Term : Ctx → Ty → Type (typed)
Typing relation HasType (9-rule inductive) Built into Term
Variables Nat + lookup proof Mem τ Γ (proof IS the variable)
Preservation 40-line theorem Free (type signature)
Substitution lemma 130 lines Not needed (function is typed)
Weakening 30-line theorem One-line function
Canonical forms Separate lemma Pattern matching
Ill-typed terms Representable Unrepresentable
Total Lean4 LOC ~400 ~180

What we gained

Dependent de Bruijn cuts the formalization roughly in half. Preservation, the substitution lemma, weakening, and canonical forms all either vanish or become trivial. The code is shorter and carries more information.

What we lost

Terms are harder to construct: you need membership proofs for variables instead of raw numbers. Metaprograms that generate terms (compilers, for example) need to produce typed output, which can be more work. And the indexed type Term : Ctx → Ty → Type requires a type system (like Lean4’s) that supports indexed inductive families.

The deeper lesson

This isn’t just a proof technique. It’s a design principle: encoding invariants into your data structures eliminates entire categories of bugs. Rust’s ownership system prevents use-after-free not by checking at runtime, but by making dangling pointers unrepresentable in the type system. The same principle is at work here: we made ill-typed terms unrepresentable, and preservation became free.

When you design a system, ask: what invariants could I encode into the types? Every invariant you encode is an invariant you never have to check, test, or prove.

The Lean4 Code

The complete formalization lives in lecture-projects/stlc-intrinsic/:

cd lecture-projects/stlc-intrinsic && lake build
File Contents LOC
Syntax.lean Ty, Mem, Term, Value ~35
Renaming.lean Typed renaming, weakening ~25
Substitution.lean Typed substitution, substTop ~30
Semantics.lean Step (preservation is the signature) ~30
Progress.lean Progress theorem ~55
Soundness.lean MultiStep, type soundness ~15

Every theorem is fully proved with zero sorry.

item.title: Project 4: Church Encoder
item.description:
Due: Tuesday, April 21, 11:59PM

Starter code: p4-public.tar.gz

Submit via autograde.org. If you are not enrolled in the course, you can still work through this project using the public starter code and tests above.

Lecture notes: Church Encoding

In this project, you will write a Church encoder: a compiler from a large subset of Scheme to lambda-calculus. In other words, you will transform inputs like '(let ([x 0]) x) to outputs like '((lambda (x) x) (lambda (f) (lambda (x) x))). Your output will be quoted data in the lambda-calculus: the test infrastructure will then interpret this into a Racket lambda by using eval.

It is crucial to understand that you are not building an interpreter, as in project 3. Instead, you are building a compiler. Your project will translate the input language into the lambda-calculus by removing each Racket form, one-by-one, and encoding them in the lambda-calculus.

To understand the encodings, please read through the Church Encoding lecture notes, the posted course slides, the course videos, and the recorded class lectures on Blackboard. We have covered many of the forms already: the main challenge in this project is translating the “on paper” knowledge into a working compiler.

The central challenge with this project is debugging. You should try to learn a debugging methodology that works for you. I recommend calling your compiler on smaller and smaller programs until you recognize which part is incorrect. Work to gradually whittle down the test cases until you isolate precisely what is wrong.

Good luck!

The Language: Syntax

Below is the full syntax of the language you must support:

e ::= (letrec ([x (lambda (x ...) e)]) e)
    | (let ([x e] ...) e)
    | (let* ([x e] ...) e)
    | (lambda (x ...) e)
    | (e e ...)
    | x
    | (and e ...) | (or e ...)
    | (if e e e)
    | (prim e) | (prim e e)
    | datum

datum ::= nat | (quote ()) | #t | #f
nat ::= 0 | 1 | 2 | ...
x is a symbol
prim is a primitive operation in list prims
(define prims '(+ * - = add1 sub1 cons car cdr null? not zero?))
The following are *extra credit*: -, =, sub1

This input language has semantics identical to Scheme / Racket, except:

  • You will not be provided code that yields any kind of error in Racket
  • You do not need to treat non-boolean values as #t at if, and, or forms (Racket allows “truthy” and “falsy” values – we won’t handle those)
  • primitive operations are either strictly unary (add1 sub1 null? zero? not car cdr), or strictly binary (+ - * = cons)
  • There will be no variadic functions or applications — but any fixed arity is allowed (e.g., ((lambda l (first l)) 1 2 3) is not allowed but ((lambda (x y z) x) 1 2 3) is)

Output language

Your output must be a quoted expression in the lambda-calculus:

e ::= (lambda (x) e)
    | (e e)
    | x

Functions and Builtins

You will primarily implement the churchify function, which accepts an input in the input language above and produces an output in the lambda-calculus. churchify recognizes each form in the input language (using a match pattern) and then calls itself.

To make things easier for you, we have used a trick: the function church-compile calls churchify with a large let block to bind each of the builtins. This allows you to handle builtin operators in a relatively simple way: you can just translate (+ e0 e1) to use currying ((+ e0') e1'), where e0' and e1' are the Church encodings of e0 and e1. Then, + will be given a binding because it is wrapped in the top-level let block in church-compile.

Please think about the above paragraph until it makes sense to you: it makes handling builtins overwhelmingly simpler.

Implementation Roadmap

This project is designed so you can implement it in stages, passing more tests at each stage. The early tests (stages 1-8) test churchify directly, so you do not need church-compile or any builtins to start passing tests. Later tests (stages 9-11) go through church-compile and require builtins.

Stage 1: Variables and Natural Numbers

Tests: public-01a-nat-zero, public-01b-nat-nonzero

Start here. Implement these two match cases:

  • Variables (? symbol? x): Just return the symbol as-is. This is trivial but required for everything else.

  • Natural numbers (? natural? nat): Encode as Church numerals. A Church numeral n is (lambda (f) (lambda (x) (f^n x))) where f^n means f applied n times. For example:

    • 0 -> (lambda (f) (lambda (x) x))
    • 3 -> (lambda (f) (lambda (x) (f (f (f x)))))

    Write a helper function to produce the (f (f ... x)) part, then wrap it in the two lambdas. Remember to churchify the result.

    See the Church Encoding lecture notes for a full explanation.

Stage 2: Single-arg Lambda and Application

Tests: public-02a-lambda-id, public-02b-lambda-const

These are needed for almost everything else, so do them early.

  • Single-arg lambda (lambda (x) e): Recursively churchify the body: `(lambda (,x) ,(churchify e0))

  • Single-arg application (fun arg): Churchify both parts: `(,(churchify fun) ,(churchify arg))

Stage 3: Multi-arg Lambda and Application (Currying)

Tests: public-03a-curry-lam, public-03b-curry-app

In lambda calculus, all functions take exactly one argument. Multi-arg functions must be curried.

  • Multi-arg lambda (lambda (x y z ...) e): Curry into nested single-arg lambdas. Hint: (churchify '(lambda (x . rest) e)) -> `(lambda (,x) ,(churchify `(lambda ,rest ,e)))

  • Zero-arg lambda (lambda () e): Add a dummy parameter _.

  • Multi-arg application (f a b c ...): Curry into nested applications. (f a b c) -> (((f a) b) c). Hint: recursively churchify ((f arg) rest...).

  • Zero-arg application (f): Apply with a dummy argument (lambda (_) _).

See the Church Encoding lecture notes for the background on currying.

Stage 4: Boolean Literals

Tests: public-04a-true, public-04b-false

A Church boolean takes two thunks and calls one of them:

  • #t -> (lambda (tt ft) (tt)) (calls the true-thunk)
  • #f -> (lambda (tt ft) (ft)) (calls the false-thunk)

Hint: just churchify the lambda expression shown above. Since these use multi-arg lambdas and zero-arg application, you need stage 3 working first.

See the Church Encoding lecture notes for the full explanation of the thunk-based encoding.

Stage 5: If Expressions

Tests: public-05a-if-true, public-05b-if-false

Since a Church bool selects between two thunks:

  • (if e0 e1 e2) -> (e0 (lambda () e1) (lambda () e2))

Just churchify that expression – it’s a 3-arg application.

See the Church Encoding lecture notes for how if works with the boolean encoding.

Stage 6: Let Expressions

Tests: public-06a-let-simple, public-06b-let-empty, public-06c-let-multi

Let is syntactic sugar for lambda + application:

  • (let ([x e0]) body) -> ((lambda (x) body) e0)
  • (let ([x e0] [y e1]) body) -> ((lambda (x y) body) e0 e1)
  • (let () body) -> just body

Churchify the desugared form.

Stage 7: Let* and Null Literal

Tests: public-07a-letstar, public-07b-null

  • let*: Desugar to nested let: (let* ([x e0] rest...) body) -> (let ([x e0]) (let* (rest...) body))

  • Null '(): Encode like a boolean pair callback that calls the when-null case: (lambda (when-cons when-null) (when-null))

See the Church Encoding lecture notes for the list encoding.

Stage 8: And / Or

Tests: public-08a-and-true, public-08b-or-true, public-08c-and-false

Desugar to nested if expressions:

  • (and e0 e1 ...) -> (if e0 (and e1 ...) #f)
  • (or e0 e1 ...) -> (if e0 #t (or e1 ...))
  • Base cases: (and) = #t, (or) = #f (already provided)

See the Church Encoding lecture notes for the desugaring.

Stage 9: Arithmetic Builtins (in church-compile)

Tests: public-09a-add1, public-09b-plus, public-09c-mult, public-09d-zero-true, public-09e-zero-false, public-09f-not

Now fill in the Church-encoded definitions in church-compile:

  • add1: (lambda (n) (lambda (f) (lambda (x) (f ((n f) x)))))
  • +: (lambda (n0 n1) (lambda (f) (lambda (x) ((n1 f) ((n0 f) x)))))
  • *: (lambda (n0 n1) (lambda (f) (lambda (x) ((n0 (n1 f)) x))))
    • Warning: heed the note in the course videos: the video gets * wrong, but the slides get it right.
  • zero?: (lambda (n) ((n (lambda (_) #f)) #t))
  • not: (lambda (b) (if b #f #t))

Note: these definitions themselves use forms like #t, #f, if, and multi-arg lambdas, which churchify will process. So you need stages 1-8 working for these to work.

See the Church Encoding lecture notes for the derivation of each of these definitions.

Stage 10: List Builtins

Tests: public-10a-cons-basic, public-10b-car, public-10c-cdr, public-10d-null-true, public-10e-null-false

  • cons: (lambda (a b) (lambda (when-cons when-null) (when-cons a b)))
  • car: (lambda (p) (p (lambda (a b) a) (lambda () (lambda (x) x))))
  • cdr: Follow the same pattern as car – what changes?
  • null?: Think about what each callback should return.

See the Church Encoding lecture notes for the observer pattern behind these definitions.

Stage 11: Letrec (Y-combinator)

Tests: public-11a-letrec-basic, public-11b-letrec-recursive

To handle letrec, use the Y combinator for recursion:

  • (letrec ([f (lambda (args...) body)]) e1) -> (let ([f (Y-comb (lambda (f) (lambda (args...) body)))]) e1)

You need to define Y-comb in church-compile:

  • Y = ((lambda (u) (u u)) (lambda (y) (lambda (mk) (mk (lambda (x) (((y y) mk) x))))))

See the Church Encoding lecture notes for the full explanation of the Y combinator and how it enables recursion. The answer is surprisingly simple: you apply the Y combinator to (lambda (f) ...), then bind the result with let.

Integration Tests

The remaining tests (public-add, public-arith0, server-append, etc.) combine multiple features. Once you have stages 1-11 working, most of these should pass automatically.

Extra Credit: sub1, -, =

The sub1 (predecessor) function is significantly more complex than the other builtins. Look it up on Wikipedia if you’d like to attempt it. Interesting history:

“Be this as it may, Kleene did find a way to lambda define the predecessor function in the untyped lambda calculus, by using an appropriate data type (pairs of integers) as auxiliary device. In [69], he described how he found the solution while being anesthetized by laughing gas for the removal of four wisdom teeth.” – Henk Barendregt’s “Impact of the Lambda calculus”

Debugging Tips

  • Call your compiler on smaller and smaller programs to isolate which part is broken.
  • Use the staged tests: if public-01a-nat-zero fails, focus on your natural number encoding. If public-05a-if-true fails, look at your if/boolean encoding.
  • You can test churchify directly in the REPL: 
    > (churchify '0)
'(lambda (f) (lambda (x) x))
> (churchify '#t)
'(lambda (tt) (lambda (ft) (tt (lambda (_) _))))
  • You can evaluate and convert back: 
    > (church->nat (eval (churchify '3) (make-base-namespace)))
3
